Why profitable firms still close

Wages, suppliers and VAT fall due on fixed dates, but customer cash arrives 30–90 days later. A firm can be profitable on paper and still run out of cash.

The existing gap

GapEvidence
Low reach~45,000 UK businesses use invoice finance vs 1.57m with overdue bills (~3%, rough calc)
Entry barriersMinimum turnover £50K–£500K depending on provider
Costly for one-off useSingle-invoice finance typically 3–5% of invoice value
Lock-insMinimum monthly charges & termination fees, often 3–6 months' service charge
Law not in force yetBill caps terms at 60 days (30 public bodies), expected no earlier than 2027
Data gapGovernment holds no data on average amount owed to SMEs in overdue invoices

Sources: DBT/OSBC–London Economics (Jul 2025), R3 Q1 2026, FreeAgent, UK Finance, Spark Finance, Hansard WQ 7647.

Slide 3 · How the solution closes the gap

Each gap maps to one feature, and PayPal supplies the invoice and payout rails.

GapOur fixPayPal's utility
Entry barriers, lock-insPer-invoice funding, no contract, no minimum feeDeveloper sandbox, no bank integration to start
Slow cashAdvance after buyer confirmation (target: 24–48 hrs)Payouts sends the advance
No trusted invoice recordReal invoice with ID, buyer confirmation, delivery proofInvoicing creates, sends and reminds
Status opacityOne status trailRecording a payment marks the invoice PAID, or PARTIALLY PAID if some amount remains
Collection costBuyer pays by bank transferAPI accepts BANK_TRANSFER as a recorded payment method, avoiding the % card fee
Closures, honest framing: We cannot prove closures will fall. We can say the cash gap on a financed invoice shrinks from up to 60 days to a target of 1–2 days. Even 1% of 14,000 closures is 140 firms a year — a sensitivity example, not a forecast.

Slide 4 · Innovation and feasibility

Simple to build in 29 days, novel in how proof, risk and cash are linked.

Innovation

  1. Buyer confirmation plus delivery proof as the evidence layer — no blockchain.
  2. AI invoice extraction, duplicate/fraud checks and an explainable risk score.
  3. Pricing agent that sets fee and advance % per invoice, and chases the buyer (Agentic Commerce angle).
  4. Late-interest design: the Bill sets statutory interest at 8% above base rate, which the pool can share once enacted.

Slide 5 · Risk mitigation and strategy

Buyer acceptance is evidence, not a guarantee, so risk is controlled in layers.

RiskControl
Dispute or delivery problemDelivery/PO proof, dispute window, buyer dispute history
Buyer late or insolventBuyer credit check, advance 70–85% by score, concentration cap (max 20% of pool per buyer, assumption)
Fake or duplicate invoiceInvoice hash check, no funding without confirmation, per-SME limit
“Paid” status wrongBank-side confirmation (simulated in sandbox)
Card fee kills marginLeg 2 by bank transfer, recorded via API
Regulation (FCA, pooling, PayPal lending policy)Unverified. Simulated pool now, authorised partner later
AI error or biasExplainable score, human override, decision log

Default loss waterfall (proposed)

  1. Recourse to SME
  2. First-loss reserve of platform / financer partner
  3. Senior investor last

Strategy

  • Phase 1 — sandbox demo
  • Phase 2 — pilot with one licensed financer, 20–50 invoices
  • Phase 3 — institutional pool once loss data exists

Slide 6 · Stakeholders and business model

The fee must cover investor return, loss and cost: minimum 1.83%, assumed 3%.

Market check: total invoice-factoring charges are typically 1–5% of invoice value, with 70–90% advanced. Older sources cite investor gross yields of 8–15% with 1–3% annual losses.

Unit economics: £10,000 invoice, 60 days, 85% advance (£8,500). All assumptions.

ItemCalculation£
SME fee3% of £10,000300.00
Investor return Y10% × £8,500 × 60/365139.73
Expected loss D2% × £8,500 × 60/36527.95
Cost Fpayout 0.75 + credit data 4 + AI/compute 5 + ops 515.00
Margin M117.32
ScenarioMargin
Buyer pays on time by bank transfer+£117.32
Buyer pays via PayPal at ~2.9% + £0.30 (third-party figure, verify)−£172.98
Buyer 30 days late, platform absorbs extra investor accrual+£47.46
Buyer defaultsSee default waterfall, Slide 5
Key numbers: Break-even fee is 1.83% (zero margin) and 2.33% for £50 margin. Effective cost is about 21% annualised, so target firms that cannot get a facility. The expected-loss reserve covers only 0.33% of principal, so diversification is essential. If the platform alone bore all loss, break-even default rate is about 1.7% of invoices.

Investor return is not promised. It is the invoice discount minus losses. Legal structure (receivable purchase or loan notes) needs an FCA-authorised partner.

Slide 7 · Appendix

Pricing rule, API status, assumptions and sources.

A1. Pricing rule

X ≥ Y + F + D + M

X = SME fee, Y = investor return, F = platform cost, D = expected loss, M = margin.

A2. PayPal API status

  • Verified create/send/remind invoice, record external payment, partial-paid status
  • Documented, not fully checked Payouts, GBP/UK recipient support, webhooks
  • Unverified invoicing webhook event names, UK fee schedule, lending-flow permission

A3. Assumptions to replace with partner quotes

3% fee, 10% investor yield, 2% loss, £15 cost, 85% advance, 20% concentration cap.

A5. Demo scope

PayPal sandbox, simulated pool, no real money.

A4. Sources: DBT/OSBC London Economics (Jul 2025), R3 Q1 2026, FreeAgent, Spark Finance, law-firm summaries of the Commercial Payments Bill, PayPal developer docs and fee schedule.
